Submission-ready reproducibility release for the PL-Seq reanalysis.

This version includes the revised manuscript source and title, complete Nature-style software references, the bioRxiv PDF build workflow, seven machine-readable supplementary tables, the renamed and updated Supplementary Figure 1 catalog, updated Figure 1 timeline, and stable Zenodo concept-DOI citation metadata.

All repository safety, syntax, and reviewed-figure checksum checks passed before release. This version adds the exact AMD64 Apptainer SIF used for FASTQ alignment, BAM processing, molecule filtering, and PSI reconstruction. The binary environment is accompanied by a SHA-256 checksum, embedded image labels, a command-derived software-version report, and usage documentation. The original Apptainer definition file was not retained; therefore, the archived SIF is the authoritative record of the executed computational environment. This version adds plseq-plotting.sif , a rebuildable Apptainer environment for programmatic PL-Seq and direct-RNA figure generation. It includes Python, Matplotlib, pyGenomeTracks, R plotting packages, Pandoc, and Poppler. The image passed embedded dependency tests, PNG/PDF artifact tests, and end-to-end rendering of the seven-page, 28-gene direct-RNA atlas.

items.summary: Supporting data and analysis code for the manuscript "Lifestyle-resolved fecal viromes reveal host-associated viral reservoirs and auxiliary metabolic divergence across animal feces". The retained dataset contains 166 fecal metagenomes (110 newly generated and 56 public), 15,106 representative vOTUs and 112 candidate auxiliary gene ORF-KO records across 105 vOTUs. The five archives provide processed data and figure sources; viral and candidate auxiliary gene sequences; the original 3,845-MAG local reference collection; assemblies for all 166 retained samples; and MAG annotation/host-comparison evidence. Raw reads are available under NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA1454088 and the individual SRR/ERR accessions listed in the sample metadata. Version 1.1.0 is a documentation and Figure 1 reproducibility correction. It removes an unused constant input-target plotting-metadata column, provides observed QC yield fields, supplies Figure 1's required local source files, and documents the actual Holm/BH comparison families, Python-versus-R community-statistics implementations and KOfamScan-versus-DIAMOND evidence roles. Scientific sample membership, sequence payloads, abundance matrices, recorded KO calls and statistical result values are retained. The local MAG collection preserves original reference inputs, including two MAGs attributed to an excluded source sample; it is distinct from the 166-sample analysis subset. The deposit is not a newly validated one-command raw-read-to-figure workflow. Missing upstream processing/software provenance remains disclosed. The archived corrections do not certify that the separately submitted manuscript has already been synchronized. See README.txt and METHODS_AND_VERSION_CORRECTIONS.txt for precise scope and evidence.

items.summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. Forecasting comparisons include linear autoregression, multilayer perceptrons, and persistence baselines. Reconstruction accuracy, physical admissibility, and forecast performance are treated as distinct evaluation objectives. The archive includes: • Source code for data acquisition, representation training, posthoc analysis, frozen final evaluation, and publication rendering. • Scientific configurations and dependency specifications. • Selected trained checkpoints, POD models, fitted forecasters, latent caches, training histories, and validation analyses. • Frozen final-test outputs, comparison summaries, coverage diagnostics, and provenance records. • Numerical visual exports, software tests, and workflow documentation. The original simulation data were downloaded from The Well, specifically its active_matter dataset. We acknowledge the original simulation contributors and the developers and curators of The Well. The original HDF5 simulation files are not redistributed in this record; the repository documents their acquisition, pinned revision, and content-hash verification. The Well: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/ Associated publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00568 Dataset documentation: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/datasets/active_matter/ Last-epoch checkpoints named last.pt are excluded; selected best.pt checkpoints are retained. Publication figures, tables, numerical source data, and supplementary videos are supplied with the manuscript submission and are excluded from this archive. Their public availability follows the release of the article and its supplementary materials. The code for generating those outputs remains included. The deposited ZIP contains 1,534 files and occupies approximately 26.18 GB. The accompanying README provides the archive’s SHA-256 checksum, a contents guide, installation references, and verification limits. Packaging integrity and source-checksum checks do not constitute an independent full-data replication. Some archived provenance records retain original execution paths; independent reruns should use a separate work directory and preserve the frozen results. Development repository: https://github.com/BioDecodingLab/Physically_Constrained_Representations_of_Active_Matter

items.summary: Learned surrogates of process simulators are often evaluated on random states from plants they have already seen. This technical report compares interpolation, leave-one-case-out, and leave-one-ore-group-out evaluation for five models trained on a steady-state mineral-processing simulator. The simulator tracks mineral mass over 63 size classes, water, closed grinding circuits, and unit-level balance closure. It reports limitations against published examples alongside the comparisons. On a 3,072-state design over twelve authored cases, the multilayer perceptron gives the lowest interpolation recovery RMSE (3.38 percentage points), but has a 26.24-point mean RMSE when each case is held out. The Gaussian process has the lowest mean held-out-case RMSE (10.95 points), while the perceptron has the highest median case-fold R-squared (0.547). Under ore-group holdout, the perceptron's median recovery R-squared is 0.437 across seven groups, but varies from 0.795 for the five chalcopyrite cases to -10.2 for the two gold-in-pyrite cases. items.summary: DIGITAL TWINS AND QUALITY CONTROL FOR SMART MASK MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名: 智慧面膜製程數位孿生與品質控制極限 Digital Twins and Quality Control for Smart Mask Manufacturing at the Limit is a 777-page English prospective nonclinical research working monograph investigating whether a smart facial-mask manufacturing digital twin can retain physically meaningful quality predictions on new production lines without confusing after-the-fact data reconstruction with genuine foresight. Its scientific three-coupling is manufacturing process twins, calibrated sensor evidence, and independent batch qualification. The central challenge is a frozen-model second-line test with unknown incoming lots, calibration variation, process disturbances and physically inspected quality outcomes. The primary candidate research metric is the dimensionless normalized signed prediction deviation e_Q = (Q_pred - Q_meas)/Q_spec, where the measured and predicted quality quantity and the nonzero prespecified specification scale have the same unit. A hidden unmetered driver, local thermal hotspot, power-rail partition, stale packets, reserve deficit or failure of physical stopping defeats the claim. The supplied consensus model, dx_i/dt = -sum_j a_ij(x_i-x_j)+w_i, is used to study local agreement; agreement alone cannot prove charge conservation, battery state of charge or safe power distribution. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates examine energy-balance and signed-work integration, nodal current conservation, converter and contact losses, motor work, SOC integration and transient terminal voltage, resistor networks, rated-edge loading, droop sharing, negative incremental impedance, spectral connectivity, packet age, deadline reliability, thermal RC and Joule heating, dependent hazards, stop-energy reserve, constrained dispatch, worst-node tail risk, covariance propagation and physical safe-stop latency. items.summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. It investigates whether a frozen quantum-assisted scheduling approach can coordinate photovoltaic generation, battery storage, power converters and representative habitat service loads while preserving independently measurable energy balances and a physically enforceable safe-stop authority. The three-way research coupling is Quantum Optimization x Distributed Energy x Habitat Service Loads. All proposed tests concern isolated, unoccupied low-voltage scaled apparatus, environmental chambers, hardware-in-the-loop sources and controlled load emulators. No habitable mobile building, live human occupancy, fire or grid interconnection certification is claimed. The principal falsifiable candidate is that, with identical solar forecasts, load traces, storage capacity, computational budgets, instrument calibration and safety rules, the frozen approach improves simulation-to-bench power prediction error without increasing the number of redesigns or losing any critical protected service. The strongest baselines are competent mixed-integer energy scheduling, model-predictive control and a well-tested rule-based fallback, not unrelated structural topology optimization. Six sealed solar-load-climate briefs test cloud ramps, winter demand, overheating, outages, aged storage and telemetry failures. Hidden auxiliary supply, forecast leakage, unsafe battery reserve, infeasible QUBO decoding and unmetered quantum-cloud work are legitimate ways to refute the claim. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates develop electrical and thermal energy balances, photovoltaic current-voltage behavior, storage dynamics, charge/discharge efficiency, AC power and converter losses, protected reserves, service deficit, weather-dependent demand, rolling-horizon constraints, chance and tail-risk measures, binary scheduling, QUBO and Ising mappings, QAOA evaluation, complete quantum computation time, feasible objective gaps, locked-reference Pareto hypervolume and physical simulation-to-test uncertainty. The F38 source's DeltaHV = HV(A_new) - HV(A_base) remains a secondary multiobjective research metric; its reference point and normalization must be frozen before measurement. Each mathematical plate defines units, assumptions, a specific blind falsification and related chapters. These are established conditional relations or proposed evaluation metrics, not newly discovered laws or demonstrations of quantum advantage. Eighty-two research chapters contain 410 separately paginated investigations about power custody, solar conversion, aging batteries, critical load services, control under uncertainty, quantum-classical comparisons and cross-laboratory evidence. Two hundred individually numbered Research Gates require targeted concealed faults, strong resource-matched rival explanations and hard-stop conditions. Thirty-three distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos propose specialized metering fixtures, load-emulation references, safety devices, computation audits and successor-ready evidence interfaces. These are prospective scientific objects, not fabricated instruments or completed research discoveries. Rejected runs, solver failures, negative experiments and correctly refused commands remain within the recorded study population. This monograph is a hypothesis-forming, non-occupancy research architecture; its methods require prospective physical validation, expert mathematical review and independent replication. No integrated public-road vehicle, passenger application, vehicle type approval or automatic nano-to-car scale transfer is asserted. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen distributed cooperative exchange architecture against competent fixed-body fleet dispatch, centralized modular scheduling and metered teleoperated docking with the same material, energy, operator, station, sensing, communication and computation resources. A proposed service advantage must survive the entire population of requested jobs and attempted exchanges. The source's selective-risk model, R_sel(tau) = E[L(yhat,y) given c >= tau], is retained but always reported together with accepted-task coverage; refusing difficult requests cannot count as safety or efficiency progress. items.summary: A phase-only spatial light modulator in the pupil of a microscope objective can form hundreds to thousands of optical traps at once, but only if the phase pattern it displays is computed well: the pattern fixes how much light reaches the traps, how equal the traps are, where stray light goes, how the pattern survives a real device, and how fast it can be recomputed when traps move. items.summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical method for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation. On longer moves, with the frames that keep the peak step per frame at most 0.2 Fourier units, the bound is met on 6 and 6 of 8 seeds of two lattice moves and on 5 of 6 seeds of a rearrangement case; the seeds that miss it miss it on the phase path their end phases prescribe, and at an equal number of frames on the rearrangement linear phase interpolation leads. Both results hold in a model of a simulated device and in a transient model that we define; neither is a hardware measurement. items.summary: Online sensor telemetry feeds the digital-twin, forecasting, control, and maintenance tools of instrumented water infrastructure. Probes deployed in these assets silently accumulate drift, flatlines, volatility bursts, and outages that existing pipelines often miss, because detectors and imputers are evaluated separately and under inflated synthetic metrics, and decay is treated as isolated events. This work proposes HARDIO, a Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator, an operational data-quality framework that pairs a duration-weighted sensor decay scorecard with a per-variable, chained detector-imputer benchmark. The assignment is selected by a four-pillar composite score (operational 35%, health coverage 30%, reconstruction 20%, calibration 15%) that scores the signal an operator actually receives after detection and imputation. HARDIO processes sensor installations independently, enabling parallel execution and avoiding the need to evaluate all plant channels jointly. HARDIO is validated on the Cheles wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), a real 1,177 population-equivalent (PE) plant, over 432 days, 19 channels, and eight sensor installations. No single detector-imputer pair is best for every channel, so detection and chained imputation distribute across SAITS, KNN Residual, and LSTM-AE. Chained quality is reported for all 19 channels using 1-NRMSE; relative R² is interpreted on the 16 channels where the signal variance makes it meaningful, and 12 of these exceed R²=0.90. On the held-out final 20% of the record (12 channels in five installations), HARDIO achieves a mean chained 1-NRMSE of 0.976, within 0.0035 of a per-channel oracle, and outperforms the uniform SAITS pipeline (p=0.003). Its reconstruction performance is close to that of the strongest uniform pipelines, without a statistically significant improvement over them, and slightly below that of a single detector-imputer pair selected on validation data (0.978). The released artefact exposes the model map, confidence labels, margins, and production masks for decision support.

items.summary: Next Generation Risk Assessment (NGRA) requires the integration of increasingly heterogeneous evidence from New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), computational models, chemical information, biological mechanisms and exposure assessment. RISK-HUNT3R WP9 has addressed a fundamental challenge for this transition: how to organise, connect and reuse diverse scientific information so that it can support transparent, reproducible and human-relevant safety assessment. The RISK-HUNT3R Knowledge Infrastructure provides a FAIR-oriented digital environment for managing and connecting experimental data, methods, compounds, computational resources and mechanistic knowledge. Its architecture combines harmonised data and metadata templates, controlled vocabularies and ontologies, compound and methods databases, BioStudies and EdelweissData integration, knowledge graphs, computational tools, AI assistance resources and cloud-based services. Together these resources support the progression from data capture and curation to analysis, mechanistic interpretation and evidence integration. The infrastructure has been deployed across distributed project partners to support collaborative research and reuse of RISK-HUNT3R and legacy EU-ToxRisk resources. A central principle emerging from this work is that effective NGRA infrastructure must support more than FAIR data. Methods, models, workflows, provenance, applicability and uncertainty also need to be captured so that scientific results can be interpreted within their Context of Use and assembled into evidence supporting a decision. Resources including ToxTemp, compound and methods databases, knowledge graphs, EdelweissData and ASPA-based workflows provide complementary components of this evolving evidence architecture. The resulting infrastructure provides both an operational resource for RISK-HUNT3R and a foundation for future development. By connecting data, methods, models and mechanistic knowledge through interoperable digital resources, RISK-HUNT3R demonstrates a pathway from fragmented NAM outputs towards reusable evidence workflows supporting transparent NGRA.
items.title: From NAM Data to Trusted Evidence: RISK-HUNT3R Knowledge Infrastructure for Next Generation Risk Assessment

The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow.
